situation.summary: Tenant Iven Rell reported a damp patch and occasional drips from the kitchen ceiling on 10 June 2025. Contractor Kellan Orve found moisture at a compression joint above the ceiling hatch on 11 June, and the landlord authorised only the quoted plumbing scope on 12 June. At the 13 June visit he saw a pale, fibrous-looking lining behind the ceiling board that cannot be identified visually, so he stopped and left without opening the ceiling. The tenant reported a small drip when the kitchen tap was used that morning and has stopped using it. The repair is stalled. The landlord has been asked for a decision on further assessment and scope (E024), and no cost, timing or appointment is agreed.

decision.message:
ESCALATION: 16 Brindlewick Mews, Fenbarrow. Kitchen ceiling leak, repair stopped on site because of an unidentified lining.

What is wrong: The tenant, Iven Rell, reported a damp patch and drips above the kitchen sink on 10 June (E001). On 11 June Kellan Orve (Mossbarrow Pipe Services) saw moisture at a compression joint above the ceiling hatch while the tap was running. The hatch is too small for him to reach the joint (E009, E011). The landlord, Ossa Fenlow, authorised the quoted plumbing scope up to the estimate amount. That scope is: isolate the pipe, open about 30 cm of ceiling lining, replace the joint and make the opening safe. She asked to be contacted before any increase in scope or cost (E011, E013, E014). The estimate excludes investigation, testing, removal and disposal of suspect material (E011).

At the return visit on 13 June at 10:40, Kellan saw a pale, fibrous-looking lining behind the painted ceiling board. He cannot identify it. The planned opening would mean drilling or cutting near it (E017). I told him not to disturb it and not to drill, cut, sample or remove anything. He confirms none of that has happened and he has left the ceiling unopened (E018, E023). He cannot price work involving the lining or say what assessment it needs (E023). Neither the landlord nor the building manager has any survey or record of ceiling work (E006, E013, E022).

Current risk: The leak recurred when the kitchen tap was used on the morning of 13 June. The tenant has stopped using that tap and has not touched the hatch. The ceiling is not visibly sagging (E020). The joint is still unrepaired. On 10 June the sockets were reported dry and there is no light directly below the patch (E003); this has not been rechecked since. The tenant has told us a young child lives at the flat (E007). Do not pass this on beyond need (E004).

Landlord position: She has stated her authority covers the plumbing work only, not a specialist material assessment. She wants the likely cost and timing before she considers any further spend (E022). On 13 June at 15:26 we asked her for a decision on further assessment or repair scope. No cost, appointment or approval has been agreed (E024).

Decisions needed from you:
1. Who should identify the lining (which qualified assessor), and how do we get a cost and timing to put to the landlord (E022)?
2. What interim protection is needed while the joint stays unrepaired? For example: can the affected pipe be isolated at an accessible point, within the approved scope and without touching the ceiling or lining? Only Kellan or another qualified person can confirm this.
3. Does the landlord need to be told anything about urgency, given that the leak is active and the repair is blocked?

Already done in this turn: interim safety advice sent to the tenant by Portal, promising an update by Monday 16 June 2025.
Open item: the affected-area photographs requested from the contractor (E008) are not on file.
Note: the building manager's communal roof inspection was planned for the week after 10 June (E006). Its result may bear on the source of the leak.

Nothing beyond the quoted plumbing scope is authorised. No disturbance of the lining is authorised.
decision.rationale: The authorised repair cannot go ahead safely. The access route runs past a lining that nobody can identify, and the instructed contractor cannot price or specify the assessment it needs (E017, E023). The leak is still active when the tap is used (E020), so this is water through a ceiling and not a routine wait. The landlord has refused to extend authority until she has a cost and timing (E022), and the only contractor on the job cannot supply either. Moving forward needs safety judgement (whether and how to commission a material assessment, and interim isolation) and a sourcing decision that I am not authorised to make. Waiting on E024 would leave a live leak with no plan. Chasing the landlord makes no sense because she asked us for information we do not have. Sending a second contractor or an assessor would mean spending money without approval. The tenant is exposed now, so the interim safety advice goes out in the same turn.
decision.expectedOutcome: A senior person takes ownership. They decide how a qualified identification of the lining is sourced and costed for the landlord, and whether interim isolation is possible. The tenant has safety advice and a firm update date.

decision.message:
Escalation: kitchen ceiling leak, 16 Brindlewick Mews, Fenbarrow. Tenant: Iven Rell. Landlord: Ossa Fenlow. Contractor: Kellan Orve, Mossbarrow Pipe Services.

What is wrong:
- On 11 June the contractor saw moisture at a compression joint above the kitchen ceiling hatch while the tap was running. He could not reach the joint through the hatch (E009).
- His estimate covers isolating the pipe, opening about 30 cm of ceiling lining and replacing the joint. It excludes investigating, testing, removing or disposing of any suspect material (E011).
- The landlord approved that plumbing scope only, up to the estimate, and asked to be contacted before any increase in scope or cost (E013). The contractor was told the same (E014).
- On 13 June at 10:40 the contractor was on site and saw, through the hatch, a pale, fibrous-looking lining behind the painted ceiling board. He cannot identify it. The planned opening would mean drilling or cutting near it (E017).
- We told him not to disturb, drill, cut, sample or remove anything (E018). He left without opening the ceiling. He confirms none of those things was done. He says he cannot price work involving the lining or say what assessment is needed (E023).

Where things stand with the landlord:
- On 13 June the landlord said her approval covered only the plumbing work, not a specialist material assessment. She wants the likely cost and timing before she considers more spend (E022).
- We asked her for a decision at 15:26 on 13 June (E024). We cannot give her a cost or timing yet because no specialist has been identified or priced.

Decisions needed from you:
1. Whether to commission a qualified assessment to identify the lining, which specialist to use, and how to get a price and timing to put to the landlord.
2. Whether the area stays closed until then, and whether any interim step is needed for the active leak (for example, the contractor isolating the pipe without touching the ceiling). This would need the landlord's agreement.
3. Whether the situation in the flat, with a recurring leak and a child present, needs any further safety response.

Nothing beyond the original plumbing quote is approved. No appointment, cost or completion date has been promised to anyone.

Photographs of the affected area were requested from the contractor on 10 June (E008) and are not on file. They should be obtained for the landlord and the assessor.

Today I have told the tenant that the case is being reviewed and that they will hear from us by Monday 16 June 2025.
decision.rationale: The repair cannot go ahead as approved. The planned ceiling opening would disturb an unidentified fibrous lining, and the contractor has stopped work and cannot price or specify an assessment (E017, E023). The landlord has refused to treat a material assessment as covered by her approval and wants the cost and timing first (E022). Nobody in the records can supply that cost, so the agency needs someone to decide who identifies the material and how. Meanwhile there is an active leak that recurs when the tap is used (E020), in a home with a young child (E007). The manual's triggers point to escalation rather than waiting or chasing: a possible hazardous material with no safe way to retry the work, an active leak, a vulnerable occupant, and spend or scope beyond what was approved. The landlord was asked at the decision moment (E024), so chasing her now would be premature. Under refinement 6, the routine tenant update goes out in this same turn.

final.message:
Escalation: kitchen ceiling leak, 16 Brindlewick Mews, Fenbarrow. Tenant: Iven Rell. Landlord: Ossa Fenlow. Contractor: Kellan Orve, Mossbarrow Pipe Services.

What is wrong:
- On 11 June the contractor saw moisture at a compression joint above the kitchen ceiling hatch while the tap was running. He could not reach the joint through the hatch (E009).
- His estimate covers isolating the pipe, opening about 30 cm of ceiling lining and replacing the joint. It excludes investigating, testing, removing or disposing of any suspect material (E011).
- The landlord approved that plumbing scope only, up to the estimate, and asked to be contacted before any increase in scope or cost (E013). The contractor was told the same (E014).
- On 13 June at 10:40 the contractor was on site and saw, through the hatch, a pale, fibrous-looking lining behind the painted ceiling board. He cannot identify it. The planned opening would mean drilling or cutting near it (E017).
- We told him not to disturb, drill, cut, sample or remove anything (E018). He left without opening the ceiling. He confirms none of those things was done. He says he cannot price work involving the lining or say what assessment is needed (E023).
- No survey or record of ceiling work is held by the landlord (E013, E022) or the building manager (E006).

Who is affected:
- The leak came back when the kitchen tap was used on the morning of 13 June. The tenant has stopped using that tap and has not touched the hatch. The ceiling is not visibly sagging (E020).
- A young child lives in the flat (E007).
- The tenant reported on 10 June that the sockets were dry and there is no light fitting directly below the patch (E003). Nothing has been confirmed about the electrics since then.
- The building manager says a communal roof inspection was planned for the week after 10 June (E006).

Where things stand with the landlord:
- On 13 June the landlord said her approval covered only the plumbing work, not a specialist material assessment. She wants the likely cost and timing before she considers more spend (E022).
- We asked her for a decision at 15:26 on 13 June (E024). We cannot give her a cost or timing yet because no specialist has been identified or priced.

Decisions needed from you:
1. Whether to commission a qualified assessment to identify the lining, which specialist to use, and how to get a price and timing to put to the landlord.
2. Whether the area stays closed until then, and whether any interim step is needed for the active leak (for example, the contractor isolating the pipe without touching the ceiling). This would need the landlord's agreement.
3. Whether the situation in the flat, with a recurring leak and a child present, needs any further safety response.

Nothing beyond the original plumbing quote is approved. No appointment, cost or completion date has been promised to anyone.

Photographs of the affected area were requested from the contractor on 10 June (E008) and are not on file. They should be obtained for the landlord and the assessor.

Today I have told the tenant that the case is being reviewed and that they will hear from us by Monday 16 June 2025.
final.rationale: The repair cannot go ahead as approved. The planned ceiling opening would disturb an unidentified fibrous lining, and the contractor has stopped work and cannot price or specify an assessment (E017, E023). The landlord has refused to treat a material assessment as covered by her approval and wants the cost and timing first (E022). Nobody in the records can supply that cost, so the agency needs someone to decide who identifies the material and how. Meanwhile there is an active leak that recurs when the tap is used (E020), in a home with a young child (E007). The manual's triggers point to escalation rather than waiting or chasing: a possible hazardous material with no safe way to retry the work, an active leak, a vulnerable occupant, and spend or scope beyond what was approved. The landlord was asked at the decision moment (E024), so chasing her now would be premature. Under refinement 6, the routine tenant update goes out in this same turn.
final.expectedOutcome: A manager or safety lead takes ownership. They decide how the lining will be identified and arrange a specialist price and timing to put to the landlord. They also decide the interim safety position for the leak. The tenant gets a dated update.
boundaries: This escalation does not identify the lining or say whether it is hazardous.
No assessment, ceiling opening, pipe isolation or extra spend is approved; the landlord approved only the original plumbing quote.
No repair date or cost has been promised to the tenant or the landlord.
The source of the leak has been seen at the joint but not confirmed; the communal roof and stack have not been ruled out.
Sending the tenant update does not confirm the tenant has read it.

Answer the landlord's request for cost and timing (E022) once a figure exists.
Ask the building manager for the result of the communal roof inspection.
Re-instruct the plumbing repair only once the material is identified and any change in scope or cost is approved.
Update the tenant by Monday 16 June 2025.
